newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Canada, U.S. wheat officials to speak in Brazil.
newsitem.headline: Canada, U.S. wheat officials to speak in Brazil.

text.p: Officials from the Canadian Wheat Board and the North American Export Grain Association (NAEGA) will be amongst the speakers at a conference here November 25-26, a milling association said.

Three representatives from the Canadian Wheat Board, including Commissioner Richard Klassen, will talk on the country's wheat harvest while NAEGA's Terry Garvert will speak on the U.S. wheat situation, said the Brazilian Association of Wheat Industries (Abitrigo) organising the event.
Also included on the speakers' list is Herve Limon, vice-president of Tradigrain, Geneva, and Klaus Hartges, general manager of Alfred Toepfer International who will talk on the international market.
Felipe Sola, Argentina's Agriculture Secretary, is also scheduled to give a speech on the Argentine market.

Brazil, Argentina's neighbour and Mercosul partner, has already bought around one million tonnes wheat from the new Argentine crop and should buy a total of around five million tonnes, said Abitrigo's president Antenor Barros Leal.

This would represent virtually all of Brazil's import needs for 1997 but some wheat may still be brought in for quality reasons from Canada and the U.S. although much will depend on prices, Leal said.
"I think it will be very difficult for us to buy wheat from other origins unless they lower their prices," Leal said.
Brazil's harvest has seen a dramatic increase in size in 1996 to around 2.7 million tonnes but of this only 1.5 million to two million tonnes will be of millable quality, Leal said.
Most of this is likely to be bought through a new system devised by the government to guarantee minimum prices for farmers but which relieves the government of storage costs.
Under the scheme, wheat is put up for auction to millers who bid not at an outright price but at a subsidy.
The miller then pays the government the minimum price of 157 reais ($152.43) minus the subsidy while the government pays the farmer the full minimum price.
The first auction under the new system was held yesterday and resulted in the sale of less than five percent of the 100,000 tonnes on offer.
However interest is likely to improve as sales continue and millers become more confident the system will work, Leal said.
-- Caroline Bulloch, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
